and the dearest, are loosed and where we stand confronted
by God alone. We must come into the presence of God bared
and naked, divested of all to which we would fain cling,
stripped of the rags with which we would cover ourselves, so
that we might win an understanding and consciousness of
our true being. This is a terrible, stark loneliness frightening
to the natural man; and the God who meets us in such loneli-
ness may wear to us the appearance of the annihilating
power of death. We must be ready to endure His consuming
glance, and to be nothing in His sight. We must be prepared
as it were to leave the gaily-coloured and noisy world and
to wander into the wilderness; for what R. M. Rilke says
in his Book of Hours is indeed true of God: "Thou art
the miracle in the desert which strikes lost and lonely
exiles."
Let us remind ourselves once more of this: "that day"
which spells freedom is also according to the word of Jesus
Easter Day, the Day of Resurrection, the day which follows
on the crucifixion. "You have sorrow now" —it is the sorrow
of the passion, of the cross, by which all desires and hopes are
destroyed. "But I will see you again and your hearts will
rejoice." The triumphant certitude of the resurrection is to
be bestowed on the grief of the cross. And only he who is
ready to enter with Jesus into the dread hour of God-
forsakenness on the cross, will also be allowed to share in the
joy of the Risen Saviour. To share in the cross of Christ,
however, means to surrender our wishes and plans to the
will of God, so that we place under the shadow of the cross
all that concerns us, both our hopes and our work. This
means that we enter the ultimate solitude of man before God,
and, as Paul says, that we decree the sentence of death on
ourselves, so that we put our trust not in ourselves but in
God who raises the dead (2 Cor. I: 9).
From such solitude we must return to our normal life;
but the fact that we have tarried there and ever and again
tarry there, must stamp our life with a distinctive character.
